source_scope: Diseases of Swine, 11th Edition, pages 601-800 markdown extraction
note: These are paraphrased operational facts derived from pages 601-800. They should be reviewed before insertion into exports/knowledge_facts.json.

candidate_facts.subject: swine influenza A virus
candidate_facts.object: Swine influenza cannot be confirmed from fever, cough, dyspnea, or cranioventral viral pneumonia alone; confirmation requires virus isolation, antigen or nucleic-acid detection, or appropriate serologic evidence.

candidate_facts.subject: swine influenza A virus acute diagnosis
candidate_facts.object: IAV-S detection is most reliable during the febrile acute period using nasal or pharyngeal swabs, trachea, lung, bronchoalveolar lavage, or related respiratory tissues, with samples kept cold and submitted promptly.

candidate_facts.subject: IAV-S oral fluids
candidate_facts.object: Oral fluids can screen populations for IAV-S by RT-PCR, but virus isolation and sequencing are generally less successful than from individual acute respiratory specimens.

candidate_facts.subject: IAV-S inactivated vaccines
candidate_facts.object: Inactivated IAV-S vaccines mainly induce HA-directed serum antibodies, so strain match matters and clinical lung disease may be reduced more than nasal shedding or transmission.

candidate_facts.subject: IAV-S vaccine-associated enhanced respiratory disease
candidate_facts.object: VAERD has been described when pigs vaccinated with whole-virus inactivated vaccine are challenged with sufficiently drifted heterologous strains of the same HA subtype.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine rubulavirus blue eye disease
candidate_facts.object: Blue eye disease should be considered when piglet encephalitis or mortality occurs with corneal opacity, reproductive loss, and boar orchitis or epididymitis; PRV and PRRSV remain important differentials.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine rubulavirus blue eye disease
candidate_facts.object: For suspected blue eye disease, brain is the preferred tissue for virus isolation or antigen/nucleic-acid detection, while paired serum samples can support serologic confirmation.

candidate_facts.subject: Menangle virus reproductive disease
candidate_facts.object: Menangle virus should be a rare differential when litters contain mummified fetuses of varying size, stillborn piglets, congenital defects, and reduced liveborn pigs, with PPV and other viral reproductive agents considered first.

candidate_facts.subject: Nipah virus in pigs
candidate_facts.object: Suspected Nipah virus in pigs is not a routine farm-management problem; it requires high-consequence zoonotic disease precautions and official diagnostic involvement.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine parvovirus reproductive disease
candidate_facts.object: PPV reproductive disease is mainly expressed as fetal-age-dependent embryonic death, return to estrus, small litters, mummification, stillbirths, and SMEDI-like outcomes rather than prominent maternal illness.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine parvovirus prevention
candidate_facts.object: PPV control depends on ensuring susceptible gilts have immunity before breeding; naive breeding animals are the key risk group.

candidate_facts.subject: classical swine fever
candidate_facts.object: CSF expression varies with virus virulence and host factors, so atypical or mild presentations do not exclude infection when epidemiologic or clinicopathologic suspicion exists.

candidate_facts.subject: classical swine fever
candidate_facts.object: CSF must be differentiated from ASF, septicemic bacterial diseases, PRRSV, PDNS, erysipelas, salmonellosis, and other hemorrhagic or reproductive conditions using laboratory confirmation.

candidate_facts.subject: atypical porcine pestivirus
candidate_facts.object: APPV is most relevant to congenital tremor type A-II in newborn pigs and should not be overextended to unrelated adult neurologic syndromes without supporting evidence.

candidate_facts.subject: foot-and-mouth disease in pigs
candidate_facts.object: FMD-like vesicles or erosions in pigs must be differentiated from SVD, Senecavirus A, vesicular stomatitis, vesicular exanthema, and noninfectious lesions by official laboratory testing.

candidate_facts.subject: foot-and-mouth disease in pigs
candidate_facts.object: Suspected FMD in pigs should trigger movement restriction, official reporting/testing, and avoidance of routine treatment or marketing advice.

candidate_facts.subject: Senecavirus A
candidate_facts.object: Senecavirus A vesicular lesions in pigs are clinically indistinguishable from FMD, SVD, VS, and VES, so laboratory testing is mandatory before assigning cause.

candidate_facts.subject: encephalomyocarditis virus
candidate_facts.object: EMCV should be considered in compatible outbreaks with sudden death, myocarditis, neonatal losses, or reproductive problems, especially when rodent exposure and lesion distribution fit.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine teschovirus
candidate_facts.object: Porcine teschovirus may be associated with polioencephalomyelitis and other syndromes, but diagnosis should connect viral detection to neurologic lesions and exclude other causes.

candidate_facts.subject: PRRSV
candidate_facts.object: PRRSV should be evaluated as a herd-level reproductive and respiratory disease whose clinical expression depends on strain, immunity, coinfections, herd flow, and management.

candidate_facts.subject: PRRSV ORF5 and RFLP typing
candidate_facts.object: PRRSV ORF5 sequence or RFLP labels are useful descriptors but should not be treated as direct guarantees of virulence, vaccine protection, or complete genetic relatedness.

candidate_facts.subject: PRRSV diagnosis
candidate_facts.object: PRRSV testing may use serum, oral fluids, processing fluids, tissues, bronchoalveolar lavage, fetal tissues, or reproductive materials depending on whether the question is acute infection, exposure, surveillance, reproductive loss, or strain monitoring.

candidate_facts.subject: PRRSV control
candidate_facts.object: PRRSV control requires a herd program such as biosecurity, acclimatization, herd closure, surveillance, vaccination decisions, test-and-removal, or elimination planning rather than single-animal treatment alone.

candidate_facts.subject: swinepox
candidate_facts.object: Swinepox should be considered for self-limiting papular, pustular, and crusting lesions on sparsely haired skin, while exudative epidermitis, mange, insect bites, and vesicular diseases remain differentials.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine rotavirus diarrhea
candidate_facts.object: Rotavirus diarrhea is a malabsorptive enteric syndrome with villous injury; diagnosis should account for age, immunity, fecal or intestinal samples, and common coinfections with other neonatal or post-weaning enteric agents.

candidate_facts.subject: porcine endogenous retroviruses
candidate_facts.object: Porcine endogenous retroviruses are primarily relevant to xenotransplantation and biosafety risk assessment rather than routine swine herd disease diagnosis.

candidate_facts.subject: vesicular stomatitis in pigs
candidate_facts.object: Vesicular stomatitis can resemble FMD and other vesicular diseases in pigs; clinical appearance alone is insufficient and official laboratory differentiation is required.

candidate_facts.subject: rabies virus in pigs
candidate_facts.object: Rabies is uncommon in pigs but must remain a public-health-critical neurologic differential when exposure history and signs are compatible.

candidate_facts.subject: Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae
candidate_facts.object: App should be suspected in compatible outbreaks with acute fever, dyspnea, cyanosis, sudden death, and fibrinohemorrhagic necrotizing pleuropneumonia, but confirmation requires appropriate laboratory workup.

candidate_facts.subject: Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae antimicrobial treatment
candidate_facts.object: Early antimicrobial therapy may reduce App mortality, but it does not eliminate herd infection or carrier pigs and must follow susceptibility, label, withdrawal, and stewardship constraints.

candidate_facts.subject: Actinobacillus pleuropneumoniae vaccines
candidate_facts.object: App vaccines can reduce clinical signs and lung lesions, but serotype match and product type matter and vaccination should not be assumed to eliminate carriers.

candidate_facts.subject: Actinobacillus suis
candidate_facts.object: Actinobacillus suis can cause septicemia, sudden death, pneumonia, pleuritis, arthritis, meningitis, endocarditis, and reproductive problems, so culture and lesion distribution are needed to separate it from App, S. suis, Glasser's disease, erysipelas, and salmonellosis.

candidate_facts.subject: Bordetella bronchiseptica
candidate_facts.object: Bordetella bronchiseptica can cause sneezing, nasal discharge, dry cough, nonprogressive turbinate atrophy, and bronchopneumonia, but it often occurs with other respiratory pathogens and its causal role must be assessed in context.

candidate_facts.subject: progressive atrophic rhinitis
candidate_facts.object: Severe progressive atrophic rhinitis or snout distortion should not be attributed to Bordetella alone without considering toxigenic Pasteurella multocida coinfection.

candidate_facts.subject: Bordetella bronchiseptica diagnosis
candidate_facts.object: Bordetella diagnosis may use nasal swabs, postmortem lung washings, biopsy specimens, selective culture, PCR, and turbinate scoring when rhinitis severity is the question.

candidate_facts.subject: Bordetella bronchiseptica vaccination
candidate_facts.object: Bordetella bacterins can reduce disease manifestations such as turbinate atrophy, but vaccinated pigs may still become colonized and shed the organism.
